title: What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside Every Segment — Products, Customers & Real-World Examples

epigraph.quote: “Going forward, the contribution of facades will increase gradually leading to better execution and margin profiles for the company.”
epigraph.author: Aluwind Infra-Tech, FY26 results press release, 5 May 2026

web_blocks.html: Aluwind designs, fabricates, supplies and installs aluminium-and-glass building envelopes. In practice that is four product families: system windows and doors; unitised and semi-unitised curtain walls (factory-built glass-and-aluminium wall panels that are lifted into place on a tower); other architectural works such as aluminium composite panel (ACP) cladding, skylights, canopies, railings and spider glazing; and, since FY26, tolling, meaning contract manufacturing for another company’s orders [1]. The accounts do not report these separately. The FY26 note splits revenue only into “aluminium windows and façade work” and “tolling”, and the half-year filing states that the company has one reportable segment because tolling is below 10% of revenue [1][5]. Anyone claiming a window-versus-façade revenue percentage for Aluwind is estimating; I will say “not disclosed” where that is the case.

web_blocks.takeaway: Windows and façade are one line. The only new revenue stream, tolling, is 1.1% of sales, and Clean-Tech has not billed anything; so the business is still a project contractor whose mix cannot be verified from filings. Figures from the FY26 annual report (note 21) [1].

web_blocks.title: Windows and doors, including the Eternia channel

web_blocks.html: A system window is an engineered product: aluminium sections from a branded range, a gasket and hardware kit, tested for wind, water and air leakage. Aluwind makes these for developers of apartment towers. The customer’s problem is volume with repeatability: hundreds or thousands of identical openings per tower, delivered tower by tower as construction advances. The Godrej Reserve order shows the model end to end. On 16 January 2026 Godrej Properties awarded the design, manufacture, fabrication and supply of aluminium windows, deck railing, glazing and louvers for Towers 3, 4 and 5 at Kandivali, Mumbai, for ₹43.15 Cr excluding GST, to be finished within 38 months of the notice [14]. Aluwind’s described process runs: shop drawings approved by consultants, material purchase through its ERP system, pretreatment and powder coating of the extrusions, CNC cutting and machining, assembly, dispatch in its own vehicles and installation by contract labour [3]. Pricing is contractual and fixed, with revenue booked on percentage of completion [1]. At ₹43.15 Cr over 38 months, the order bills about ₹1.14 Cr a month.

The Eternia channel is the same product under a premium brand. In Tata Realty’s Tata Serein project in Thane, Aluwind installs the Eternia window system under a ₹7.5 Cr order due by the end of 2026 [19]. Capacit’e Infraprojects ordered Eternia system windows for the MHADA BDD Chawl redevelopment in Worli, Mumbai, for ₹8.74 Cr [18]. The largest window-led award is Runwal Realty’s October 2024 acceptance for aluminium windows across 19 towers in Mumbai, Thane and Pune, about 14.5 lakh sq ft, plus façade work, worth ₹89.9 Cr over three years [17]. That works out to at most about ₹620 per sq ft including the façade element, against about ₹1,100 per sq ft for the older Birla Vanya job (₹22 Cr for about 2,00,000 sq ft of system windows) [1]. Prices per sq ft differ sharply with window grade, so that comparison is a range, not a benchmark. Lodha’s Bhandup award of 28 July 2026 (₹12.59 Cr, finishing 1 July 2028) is written as a Full Material plus Labour, item-rate contract: Aluwind supplies everything and is paid a rate per measured item, not a lump sum [15].

A curtain wall hangs from a building’s floor slabs and carries no load itself. In a unitised system the glass, aluminium frame and gaskets are assembled in the factory into storey-high panels, shipped to site and hung by crane. In a semi-unitised system the frames are fixed first and glass follows. The L&T Innovation Campus in Powai, Mumbai, is the company’s showcase: the FY26 report describes unitised façade panels of 1.5 m by 4.2 m and calls it the single largest façade order from L&T Construction [1]; Eternia’s own project page lists the campus at 36,000 m² of unitised façade [24]. The contract value is not disclosed in anything I found. The Capgemini SIPCOT campus in Siruseri, Chennai, is a second case with a known price: Vascon Engineers awarded design, supply, fabrication and erection of façade work for ₹43.03 Cr excluding GST, within 18 months of the letter of intent [16], the highest façade order in the company’s history. Eternia’s page lists a 12,200 m² unitised system at a Capgemini campus in Chennai [24]. If Aluwind’s scope is the whole area, the price is near ₹35,000 per m² (about ₹3,280 per sq ft), but the filing does not confirm that the two are the same scope.

web_blocks.title: Other architectural works, tolling and Clean-Tech

web_blocks.html: The third family covers cladding, skylights, canopies, railings and spider glazing (glass held by stainless-steel point fixings) [3]. It shows up as shorter, project-specific orders. The Mumbai International Cruise Terminal needed second-skin façade works from Ballard Pier Private Limited for ₹15.4 Cr within six months [19]. L&T Construction awarded façade and aluminium joinery for the Sabarmati depot of the Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet-train project at ₹15.61 Cr [13], façade design, supply, installation and handing over at AIIMS Madurai at ₹19.21 Cr [20], and an ancillary façade package for the Navi Mumbai airport at ₹6.23 Cr in 3.5 months [21]. Prestige Estates ordered the clubhouse and entrance lobby façade at The Prestige City, Mulund, for ₹8.30 Cr over 18 months [19]. Tolling began in FY26 under a Toll Agreement with Hindalco Industries; the company amended its charter to add job work and booked ₹1.57 Cr [1]. Management says the aim is to manufacture Eternia’s West and South India retail window orders in Aluwind’s plant [2]. Pricing is undisclosed. In a toll arrangement the customer normally supplies the metal and pays a conversion fee, so tolling revenue should carry less material cost and less cash tied up; that is my understanding of the term, not a disclosed contract term.

Aluwind Clean-Tech, formed 21 May 2025 and 60% owned, plans façade cleaning and maintenance under annual contracts, including drone cleaning of façades, solar panels and windows [1]. It had no revenue and a ₹7.46 lakh loss in FY26 and a ₹8.90 lakh loss in H1 FY27 [1][5]. No customer or contract is named in the filings, so there is no worked example to give. Building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV), which are solar panels built into a façade, are described as research; no BIPV order has been disclosed [2]. Both lines are options, not revenue.

web_blocks.takeaway: The fifteen disclosed orders total ₹322.55 Cr. By my classification ₹142.85 Cr (44%) is façade and ₹179.70 Cr (56%) is windows. L&T entities hold ₹76.12 Cr (24%); Maharashtra is 65%, Tamil Nadu 30% and Gujarat 5%.

web_blocks.html: Customer type and geography are therefore mixed. Residential developers (Godrej, Runwal, Lodha, Tata Realty, Prestige) place window orders. Contractors and corporate owners (L&T, Vascon for Capgemini) place façade orders. Institutions and infrastructure (AIIMS, the bullet train, an airport, a cruise terminal) are the third group [12][13][14][16][17][20]. The expansion into Tamil Nadu is real: Chennai, Coimbatore and Madurai orders total ₹97.31 Cr, 30% of the disclosed value, and the company has named Karnataka, Gujarat and Telangana as targets [7]. Concentration is the weak point. In FY23 the top ten customers were 67% of sales and in H1 FY24 59%, with L&T group entities about 19% in FY23 [3]. The FY26 report gives no customer table. My count of disclosed orders puts L&T at 24% of announced value, so concentration remains high; it is an estimate from announcements, not a filed ratio.

web_blocks.caption: Implied billing speed of selected orders (my arithmetic: value divided by contract period)
web_blocks.takeaway: Façade orders convert to revenue two to four times faster per month than window orders, because the contract periods are shorter for similar values.

web_blocks.html: That table is the heart of the façade-versus-window question. A façade job is larger and shorter. Material is bought early, panels are built in a factory, and revenue is booked as cost is incurred, so a façade can add ₹2 Cr or more a month to revenue and to inventory and receivables. A window job is smaller per month but stretches for two to three years, which means money is tied up for a long time and a slice of every bill (the rate is not disclosed) is held as retention until the defect-liability period ends. Retention is a customer’s withheld payment, released after the work proves sound. It stood at ₹13.68 Cr of the ₹39.05 Cr billed receivables at March 2026, against ₹1.69 Cr retention that Aluwind itself withheld from vendors [1]. Performance bank guarantees (PBGs), the bank-backed promise that the contractor will finish the job, are standard in façade tenders and weigh on credit limits [3].

So what does “the contribution of facades will increase” mean? Management links it to execution and margins [2]. I read it as three claims. First, higher engineering content should earn a higher gross margin. Second, bigger tickets spread design and project-management cost. Third, façade revenue arrives faster per rupee of order book. The evidence so far is partial: the H1 FY27 EBITDA margin was 13.4% against 12.3% in H1 FY26 (my calculation from the filings), supporting the margin claim [5]. But the same half saw billed receivables rise from ₹39.05 Cr to ₹54.70 Cr, and in FY26 inventory rose 88% while revenue rose 27% [1][5]. My judgement is that the mix shift probably lifts margin by one to two points over two years (about 55% likely), and almost certainly raises working capital needs before it lowers them. The order book of ₹300 Cr, about 2.2 times FY26 revenue, gives cover, but it only becomes cash through the process described in the next chapter [2][1].

book_paragraphs: Let me ask you to picture three places, because that is the fastest way to understand what Aluwind does. First, a half-finished residential tower in Kandivali, Mumbai. Second, a glass office campus going up in Chennai. Third, a factory shed on the Pune-Aurangabad highway. Aluwind is the company that connects the three: it makes things in the third place and hangs them on the first two.

Before we go further, a warning about what the accounts do and do not tell you. The annual report splits revenue into only two lines: aluminium windows and façade work, ₹136.99 Cr in FY26, and tolling, ₹1.57 Cr [1]. The half-year filing says the company has a single reportable segment, because tolling is below 10% of revenue [5]. So there is no official figure for how much of the ₹138.56 Cr came from windows and how much from façades. When you read a number online claiming to give that split, it is an estimate. I will tell you where I am estimating and where the company has actually told us.

Start with the tower. Godrej Properties is building Towers 3, 4 and 5 of Godrej Reserve. It needs aluminium windows, deck railings, glazing and louvers for hundreds of homes. On 16 January 2026 it gave Aluwind the job for ₹43.15 Cr excluding GST, to be completed within 38 months [14]. Think about what that means. The work will run into 2029. Each month Aluwind will deliver about ₹1.14 Cr of it, on average. The company’s own description of its process is simple. Designers draw the windows. Consultants check the drawings. Aluminium is bought, painted in a powder-coating line, cut and machined by computer-controlled equipment, assembled, loaded on Aluwind’s own trucks and fitted by labour hired for the site [3]. The price is fixed in the contract and the revenue is booked as work is done [1].

Windows are the older half of the business. They come in two flavours. A plain system window is made to a standard design. An Eternia window uses the Hindalco brand’s aluminium range, and Aluwind is the lead partner for Mumbai. Tata Realty ordered Eternia windows for its Tata Serein building in Thane for ₹7.5 Cr [19]. Capacit’e Infraprojects ordered them for a Worli redevelopment for ₹8.74 Cr [18]. The largest window award of all is Runwal Realty’s ₹89.9 Cr, announced in October 2024: windows for 19 towers, about 14.5 lakh sq ft, across Mumbai, Thane and Pune, with some façade work, to be done over three years [17]. Divide the value by the area and you get at most about ₹620 per sq ft. The older Birla Vanya job works out near ₹1,100 per sq ft (₹22 Cr for about 2,00,000 sq ft) [1]. Do not treat either as a price list; the windows differ in grade, and the Runwal figure includes façade.

Last July the company took on a different type of window job: Lodha’s Bhandup project, ₹12.59 Cr, written as full material plus labour on an item-rate basis [15]. Item rate means Aluwind is paid a set rate for each measured unit, not one lump sum. That puts quantity risk on the customer and price risk on Aluwind.

There is a smaller version of the window order too. Godrej Projects Development gave Aluwind an order for what the industry calls SITC: supply, installation, testing and commissioning of aluminium windows and railings for Godrej Gardens in Mumbai. The value was ₹7.60 Cr and the deadline 24 months from acceptance [18]. That is just ₹0.32 Cr of revenue a month. A job like this keeps a crew and a section of the factory busy for two years without ever becoming large, which is why management prefers to talk about façades.

You can see the older, finished versions of this work in the company’s own report. The Gigaplex project for K Raheja in Airoli, Mumbai, is described as a façade of 85,000 square feet. The Birla Vanya housing project took system windows over 2,00,000 square feet [1]. Both are the sort of reference a developer will ask to see before it lets a contractor bid. They also tell you something about scale: this is a company that has fitted windows on a few hundred thousand square feet of towers, not one that has built a skyline.

Now the Chennai campus. A façade is the glass-and-aluminium skin of a commercial building. Aluwind makes a type called unitised: instead of fitting glass piece by piece on site, the company builds whole storey-high panels in the factory, ships them and a crane lifts them into place. At the L&T Innovation Campus in Powai, Mumbai, the panels are 1.5 m by 4.2 m [1]. That job was the largest façade order the company had ever received from L&T Construction, and Eternia’s own project page lists the campus at 36,000 square metres [1][24]. I could not find what L&T paid. But I can tell you about another campus where the price is known. Vascon Engineers awarded the façade for the Capgemini campus at Siruseri, Chennai, for ₹43.03 Cr, to be finished in 18 months [16]. That is about ₹2.39 Cr of revenue every month, more than twice the monthly pace of the Godrej windows. Eternia’s page lists a 12,200 square-metre Capgemini campus façade in Chennai [24]. If that is the same scope, the price is near ₹35,000 per square metre. The filing does not confirm it, so treat that as a clue and not a fact.

Between the tower and the campus sits a third group: cladding, skylights, canopies, railings and the stainless-steel point-fixed glass called spider glazing [3]. Examples are small and varied. A second skin for the Mumbai cruise terminal, ₹15.4 Cr in six months [19]. Façade and aluminium work for the Sabarmati depot of the Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train, ₹15.61 Cr [13]. A façade for AIIMS Madurai, ₹19.21 Cr [20]. A façade package for the Navi Mumbai airport’s ancillary buildings, ₹6.23 Cr in 3.5 months [21]. A clubhouse and entrance lobby at Prestige City in Mulund, ₹8.30 Cr [19]. Add up the fifteen orders in the table and you get ₹322.55 Cr. By my reading, about 44% is façade and 56% is windows. L&T entities account for about 24%; Maharashtra is 65% of the value, Tamil Nadu 30% and Gujarat 5%. These are my counts from announcements, not company ratios.

Who actually pays? There are three kinds of customer. Residential developers such as Godrej, Runwal, Lodha, Tata Realty and Prestige buy windows. Contractors and corporate owners such as L&T and Vascon, acting for a campus, buy façades. Institutions and public infrastructure, including AIIMS, the bullet train, an airport and a cruise terminal, buy a bit of both [12][13][14][16][17][20]. Concentration is the question to ask here. The prospectus showed the top ten customers at 67% of FY23 sales and 59% of the first half of FY24, with L&T group entities about 19% in FY23 [3]. The FY26 report does not give a customer table. From the announcements alone, L&T entities hold about 24% of disclosed order value. Treat that as a sign that concentration is still high.

Two newer lines deserve a short mention. Tolling means making another company’s product in your factory for a fee. Aluwind signed a toll agreement with Hindalco in FY26 to build window orders for Eternia’s West and South India retail business, and it earned ₹1.57 Cr, 1.1% of revenue [1][2]. The pricing is not disclosed. In a typical toll deal the customer supplies the metal and you earn a conversion fee, so there is less cash tied up. That is my understanding, not a stated term. The second line is the subsidiary Aluwind Clean-Tech, which plans to clean and maintain façades, including by drone [1]. It has earned nothing and lost money in FY26 and H1 FY27 [1][5]. No client is named. If you are looking for a worked example of Clean-Tech, I have to tell you there isn’t one yet.

What about the order book? Management puts it at about ₹300 Cr, as of May 2026, which is 2.2 times last year’s revenue [2][1]. The phrase “order book” simply means signed work not yet billed. The useful test is how fast it turns into revenue. In the first half of FY27 the company billed ₹73.99 Cr, or about ₹12.3 Cr a month [5]. At that pace, ₹300 Cr is about 24 months of work. The disclosed orders run from 3.5 months (the airport package) to 38 months (Godrej Reserve), so the book is a mix of fast façade jobs and long window programmes. Management’s FY27 target of ₹200 Cr would need ₹16.7 Cr a month for the full year, which is why the façade share matters so much [2].

Now compare windows and façades the way a practitioner would. Look at the billing speed. A window order bills slowly over two or three years. A façade order bills two to four times faster per month. Godrej Reserve runs at ₹1.14 Cr a month, Lodha at ₹0.55 Cr, Godrej Gardens at ₹0.32 Cr. Capgemini runs at ₹2.39 Cr and the cruise terminal at ₹2.57 Cr. That is why management says façades will lift execution. A faster order uses the factory better and is finished sooner. But there is a price. A façade needs material bought early, panels built before they are hung, and a bank guarantee to bid. Customers hold back a slice of every bill, called retention, until the defect period ends. At March 2026 the customers were holding ₹13.68 Cr of Aluwind’s money, while Aluwind held back only ₹1.69 Cr from its own vendors [1].

So what does the line “the contribution of facades will increase” mean for you? Margins first. The half-year to September 2026 showed an EBITDA margin of 13.4%, against 12.3% a year earlier, by my calculation [5]. That supports management. Cash next. Over the same six months billed receivables rose from ₹39.05 Cr to ₹54.70 Cr [1][5]. That does not. My view is that the façade mix probably adds one to two points of margin over two years, with a chance of about 55%, and that it will almost certainly demand more working capital first. The ₹300 Cr order book, about 2.2 times last year’s revenue, is real cover [2][1]. It only becomes cash if customers pay, which is where we go next.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A contractor’s business is the shape of its orders. Aluwind’s orders are bigger, shorter and more geographically spread than they were two years ago, and each of those changes raises both the potential margin and the cash tied up in every job. When a company tells you its mix is improving, ask what the improvement costs in working capital, and look for the receivables line before you believe the margin line.
